units.title: PIH definition → PIH postpartum course
units.guide: Anchor every hypertensive diagnosis to accurate blood-pressure confirmation, timing relative to 20 weeks and 12 weeks postpartum, and the distinction between pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, chronic hypertension, and superimposed disease. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH definition, Chronic hypertension, Pregnancy-induced hypertension, PIH postpartum course.

units.title: Pre-eclampsia → End-organ damage → Superimposed pre-eclampsia
units.guide: Anchor every hypertensive diagnosis to accurate blood-pressure confirmation, timing relative to 20 weeks and 12 weeks postpartum, and the distinction between pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, chronic hypertension, and superimposed disease. Focus for this checkpoint: Pre-eclampsia, Proteinuria, End-organ damage. It also includes Superimposed pre-eclampsia.

units.title: Mild pre-eclampsia → Impending eclampsia
units.guide: Severity hinges on BP or severe features, not the amount of protein or edema. Recognize impending eclampsia, classify eclamptic seizures by timing, and use postpartum reassessment to distinguish transient gestational hypertension from chronic disease. Focus for this checkpoint: Mild pre-eclampsia, Severe pre-eclampsia, Severity assessment, Pathological edema, Impending eclampsia.

units.title: PIH admission → Atypical eclampsia
units.guide: Severity hinges on BP or severe features, not the amount of protein or edema. Recognize impending eclampsia, classify eclamptic seizures by timing, and use postpartum reassessment to distinguish transient gestational hypertension from chronic disease. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH admission, PIH investigations, Eclampsia, Eclampsia timing, Atypical eclampsia.

units.title: PRES & Gestational hypertension
units.guide: Severity hinges on BP or severe features, not the amount of protein or edema. Recognize impending eclampsia, classify eclamptic seizures by timing, and use postpartum reassessment to distinguish transient gestational hypertension from chronic disease. Focus for this checkpoint: PRES, Gestational hypertension.

units.title: Normal placentation & PIH pathophysiology
units.guide: Normal extravillous trophoblast converts spiral arteries into low-resistance vessels in two phases. PIH begins when remodeling fails, driving placental ischemia, antiangiogenic mediator release, endothelial leak, thrombosis, renal injury, and neurologic symptoms. Focus for this checkpoint: Normal placentation, PIH pathophysiology.

units.title: Placental ischemia & PIH mediators
units.guide: Normal extravillous trophoblast converts spiral arteries into low-resistance vessels in two phases. PIH begins when remodeling fails, driving placental ischemia, antiangiogenic mediator release, endothelial leak, thrombosis, renal injury, and neurologic symptoms. Focus for this checkpoint: Placental ischemia, PIH mediators.

units.title: PIH clinical expression → PIH cause
units.guide: Normal extravillous trophoblast converts spiral arteries into low-resistance vessels in two phases. PIH begins when remodeling fails, driving placental ischemia, antiangiogenic mediator release, endothelial leak, thrombosis, renal injury, and neurologic symptoms. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH clinical expression, Endothelial injury, Thrombosis, PIH outcomes, PIH cause.

units.title: PIH treatment principle → Cerebrovascular pathology
units.guide: Normal extravillous trophoblast converts spiral arteries into low-resistance vessels in two phases. PIH begins when remodeling fails, driving placental ischemia, antiangiogenic mediator release, endothelial leak, thrombosis, renal injury, and neurologic symptoms. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH treatment principle, Renal pathology, Cerebrovascular pathology.

units.title: PIH risk factors
units.guide: Risk rises with first or increased placental exposure, placentomegaly, autoimmune disease, demographic and vascular factors. Separate measures with a proven preventive role from those without one, and interpret uterine-artery Doppler and biomarker prediction. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH risk factors.

units.title: PIH prevention & Aspirin prophylaxis
units.guide: Risk rises with first or increased placental exposure, placentomegaly, autoimmune disease, demographic and vascular factors. Separate measures with a proven preventive role from those without one, and interpret uterine-artery Doppler and biomarker prediction. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH prevention, Aspirin prophylaxis.

units.title: PIH predictors & Uterine-artery Doppler
units.guide: Risk rises with first or increased placental exposure, placentomegaly, autoimmune disease, demographic and vascular factors. Separate measures with a proven preventive role from those without one, and interpret uterine-artery Doppler and biomarker prediction. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH predictors, Uterine-artery Doppler.

units.title: PIH evaluation & Delivery timing
units.guide: Initial PIH assessment includes targeted maternal and fundal evaluation plus a HELLP screen. Severity drives site of care and timing of delivery; fetal surveillance and umbilical-artery Doppler guide escalation in expectant management. Focus for this checkpoint: PIH evaluation, Delivery timing.

units.title: Fetal monitoring & Umbilical artery Doppler
units.guide: Initial PIH assessment includes targeted maternal and fundal evaluation plus a HELLP screen. Severity drives site of care and timing of delivery; fetal surveillance and umbilical-artery Doppler guide escalation in expectant management. Focus for this checkpoint: Fetal monitoring, Umbilical artery Doppler.

units.title: Mild PE management → Severe PE management
units.guide: Mild PE without severe features is outpatient-oriented with surveillance and education; severe PE is inpatient care. Stabilize seizures and BP first, use corticosteroids when appropriate, and treat delivery as the definitive endpoint rather than an automatic cesarean. Focus for this checkpoint: Mild PE management, Mild PE treatment, Severe PE management.

units.title: Severe PE management → Eclampsia management
units.guide: Mild PE without severe features is outpatient-oriented with surveillance and education; severe PE is inpatient care. Stabilize seizures and BP first, use corticosteroids when appropriate, and treat delivery as the definitive endpoint rather than an automatic cesarean. Focus for this checkpoint: Severe PE management, PE delivery mode, PE delivery anesthesia, Eclampsia management.

questions.q: Fill up: Blood-pressure finding defines hypertension in pregnancy in the notes is ______.
opts: At least 130/80 mmHg on one occasion
At least 160/110 mmHg on two occasions 24 hours apart
At least 150/100 mmHg after delivery only
At least 140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart
questions.exp: Hypertension is BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two readings 4 hours apart. (Book p390)

questions.q: Fill up: For BP ≥160/110 mmHg, the exception is repeat measurement ______.
questions.exp: For BP ≥160/110 mmHg, the exception is repeat measurement after 15 minutes. (Book p390)

questions.q: A 26-year-old primigravida at 8 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pih definition. According to the notes, persistent severe BP after the 15-minute repeat requires antihypertensives. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
opts: Advise that give only dietary salt restriction is the correct pih definition for this patient at this gestation
Advise that start antihypertensive treatment is the correct pih definition for this patient at this gestation
Advise that wait for a 24-hour urine result before action is the correct pih definition for this patient at this gestation
Advise that classify it as normal pregnancy is the correct pih definition for this patient at this gestation
questions.exp: Persistent severe BP after the 15-minute repeat requires antihypertensives. (Book p390)

questions.q: Fill up: Chronic hypertension is present from day 1 in ______ who was hypertensive when she conceived.
opts: BP elevation begins only after delivery
BP is elevated only during labor
A woman with hypertension conceives and BP is high from day 1
A normotensive woman first develops BP elevation after 20 weeks
questions.exp: Chronic hypertension is present from day 1 in a woman who was hypertensive when she conceived. (Book p390)

questions.q: Fill up: PIH begins after 20 weeks in ______ normotensive woman and is related to placental pathology.
opts: Hypertension occurs only during the first trimester
It is caused by maternal TSH transfer
A previously normotensive woman develops hypertension after 20 weeks due to placental pathology
questions.exp: PIH begins after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive woman and is related to placental pathology. (Book p390)

questions.q: Which statement about the postpartum course of pregnancy-induced hypertension is TRUE?
opts: Blood pressure usually normalises within 12 weeks of delivery
Blood pressure usually normalises within 48 hours of delivery
Hypertension persisting beyond 12 weeks is still called gestational hypertension
Blood pressure never returns to normal after pregnancy-induced hypertension
questions.exp: PIH usually normalises within 12 weeks of delivery; a blood pressure still raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as chronic hypertension. (Book p390)

questions.q: Which statement about Chronic hypertension — BP that remains is TRUE?
opts: A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Transient hypertension only
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Chronic hypertension
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Gestational hypertension
A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as Mild pre-eclampsia
questions.exp: A BP that remains raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as chronic hypertension. (Book p390)

questions.q: Fill up: Gestational hypertension is a blood pressure of ______ mmHg or more recorded after 20 weeks in a woman without proteinuria.
questions.exp: Gestational hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria, and it must resolve by 12 weeks postpartum to keep the label. (Book p390)

questions.q: Fill up: In the source comparison, ______ signs of end-organ damage distinguish pre-eclampsia from gestational hypertension.
opts: Elevated blood pressure alone, above 140/90 mmHg
A history of a prior pregnancy affected by hypertension
Proteinuria and/or signs of maternal end-organ damage
Onset of the hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: In the source comparison, proteinuria and/or signs of end-organ damage distinguish pre-eclampsia from gestational hypertension. (Book p390)

questions.q: Match the proteinuria test with the threshold that makes it positive — 1) 24-hour urinary protein 2) Urine protein:creatinine ratio 3) Urine dipstick used for OPD screening … A) At least 300 mg per 24 hours B) At least 0.3 C) At least +1
questions.exp: Proteinuria is 300 mg or more in 24 hours, a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 0.3 or more, and a dipstick of +1 or more for OPD screening; 24-hour urinary protein is the gold standard. (Book p391)

questions.q: Which statement about Proteinuria — urine protein creatinine is TRUE?
opts: At least 0.03 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
At least 3.0 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
At least 30 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
At least 0.3 is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
questions.exp: A urine protein:creatinine ratio ≥0.3 meets the threshold. (Book p391)

questions.q: A 32-year-old G3P1L1 at 9 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding proteinuria. According to the notes, urine dipstick of +1 or more is the stated OPD screening threshold; the notes also flag stricter NICE/ACOG use. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
opts: Advise that at least +1 is the correct proteinuria for this patient at this gestation
Advise that trace only is the correct proteinuria for this patient at this gestation
Advise that at least +4 only is the correct proteinuria for this patient at this gestation
Advise that any negative value is the correct proteinuria for this patient at this gestation
questions.exp: Urine dipstick of +1 or more is the stated OPD screening threshold; the notes also flag stricter NICE/ACOG use. (Book p391)

questions.q: Which statement about Proteinuria — Twenty four hour is TRUE?
opts: Serum uric acid only is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
24-hour urinary protein excretion is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
Urine dipstick is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
Fundus examination is the listed proteinuria as per the notes
questions.exp: Twenty-four-hour urine protein excretion is listed as the gold standard. (Book p391)

questions.q: Match the severe-feature test with its end-organ-damage threshold — 1) Platelet count 2) Serum creatinine 3) Hepatic transaminases … A) Below 1 lakh/mm³ B) At least 1.1 mg/dL C) At least twice the normal level
questions.exp: Severe features are a platelet count below 1 lakh/mm³, serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL or more, and transaminases at least twice normal. (Book p391)

questions.q: Which statement about End-organ damage — Serum creatinine 1 is TRUE?
opts: At least 0.3 mg/dL is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
At least 0.8 mg/dL only is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
At least 5 mg/dL only is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
At least 1.1 mg/dL is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
questions.exp: Serum creatinine ≥1.1 mg/dL is a listed severe feature. (Book p391)

questions.q: A 32-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding end-organ damage. According to the notes, transaminases at least two times normal are a severe feature; placental ALP normally rises in pregnancy. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
opts: Advise that transaminases at least twice normal is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation
Advise that any rise in alkaline phosphatase is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation
Advise that low bilirubin only is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation
Advise that low ldh only is the correct end-organ damage for this patient at this gestation
questions.exp: Transaminases at least two times normal are a severe feature; placental ALP normally rises in pregnancy. (Book p391)

questions.q: Which statement about End-organ damage — Pulmonary edema and is TRUE?
opts: Rh negativity and proteinuria alone is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Pulmonary edema and cerebral/visual symptoms is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Physiological pedal edema and glycosuria is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
Anemia and hyperemesis is the listed end-organ damage as per the notes
questions.exp: Pulmonary edema and cerebral or visual symptoms are listed severe features. (Book p391)

questions.q: A 36-year-old with known chronic hypertension, previously well controlled on methyldopa, is now 28 weeks pregnant. Her blood pressure has become uncontrollable and she has developed new 2+ proteinuria. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Gestational hypertension alone, since she was hypertensive before
Transient hypertension of pregnancy, needing no treatment
Mild pre-eclampsia, which carries the best prognosis
questions.exp: Superimposed pre-eclampsia is chronic hypertension with uncontrollable blood pressure, new proteinuria or end-organ damage after 20 weeks, and it carries a bad prognosis. (Book p391)

questions.q: Match the superimposed pre-eclampsia with the correct detail — 1) is aspirin considered in a woman with chronic 2) urine protein:creatinine ratio meets the listed proteinuria threshold 3) dipstick protein result is the OPD screening threshold … A) To prevent superimposed pre-eclampsia B) At least 0.3 C) At least +1
questions.exp: The source notes aspirin use to prevent superimposed PE in chronic hypertension. (Book p391)

questions.q: Match the hypertensive disorder with its definition — 1) Pre-eclampsia 2) Superimposed pre-eclampsia 3) Gestational hypertension … A) New proteinuria, hypertension or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks B) Chronic hypertension with new proteinuria or a sudden worsening of control C) Hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria that settles by 12 weeks postpartum
questions.exp: Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ involvement; superimposed disease is a change in a woman who was already hypertensive. (Book p391)

questions.q: A 32-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks has a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg with 2+ urine protein. Her platelets, creatinine and transaminases are normal and she has no headache or visual symptoms. How is this classified?
opts: Mild pre-eclampsia, the pressure being 140/90 to under 160/110
Severe pre-eclampsia on the degree of proteinuria alone
Gestational hypertension, since no end-organ damage is present
questions.exp: Mild pre-eclampsia is a blood pressure of 140/90 to under 160/110 mmHg without severe features; the degree of proteinuria does not differentiate mild from severe. (Book p392)

questions.q: Fill up: Severe PE is defined by ______ ≥160/110 or severe features/end-organ damage.
opts: BP at least 160/110 mmHg or any severe feature
questions.exp: Severe PE is defined by BP ≥160/110 or severe features/end-organ damage. (Book p392)

questions.q: All of the following are listed as NON-differentiating between mild and severe pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: A blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or higher
questions.exp: The degree of proteinuria, oliguria and IUGR are all listed as non-differentiating; a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or higher does differentiate mild from severe pre-eclampsia. (Book p392)

questions.q: Which statement about Severity assessment — Oliguria listed as is TRUE?
opts: Visual symptoms is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
End-organ damage is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
Oliguria is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
Severe BP elevation is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both
questions.exp: Oliguria is listed as non-differentiating because reduced renal perfusion may occur in both. (Book p392)

questions.q: A 24-year-old G2P1L1 at 10 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding severity assessment. According to the notes, iUGR is a non-differentiating feature in the source table. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
opts: Advise that bp ≥160/110 mmhg is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
Advise that pulmonary edema is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
Advise that severe headache is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
Advise that iugr is the correct severity assessment for this patient at this gestation
questions.exp: IUGR is a non-differentiating feature in the source table. (Book p392)

questions.q: Which statement about edema in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: Edema is pathological when it does not subside with rest and involves non-dependent parts
Edema is pathological only when it is confined to the ankles after standing
Any edema appearing in pregnancy is by definition a severe feature
Edema is always absent in pregnancy-induced hypertension
questions.exp: Pathological edema does not improve with rest and is present in dependent and non-dependent parts, unlike physiological dependent edema which settles overnight. (Book p392)

questions.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks reports a severe headache that has not responded to her usual analgesics, and her blood pressure is now 160/110 mmHg. Which feature is she showing?
opts: Impending eclampsia, from a severe headache unrelieved by usual medication
Migraine with aura, occurring independently of her pre-eclampsia
Cerebral venous thrombosis, needing immediate cranial imaging
The physiological headache of pregnancy, needing only reassurance
questions.exp: Impending eclampsia includes a severe headache not relieved by usual medication, alongside visual symptoms and epigastric pain. (Book p392)

questions.q: Fill up: Epigastric pain in impending eclampsia is attributed to a ______ that is stretching the ______.
questions.exp: Epigastric pain reflects subcapsular hematoma and stretching of the liver capsule. (Book p392)

questions.q: All of the following are listed visual warning symptoms of impending eclampsia EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The source lists diplopia, blurred vision, scotoma and blindness as warning symptoms of impending eclampsia; presbyopia needing reading glasses is not one of them. (Book p392)

questions.q: Fill up: Fundus examination is part of evaluating visual symp______ms in PIH.
questions.exp: Fundus examination is part of evaluating visual symptoms in PIH. (Book p392)

questions.q: All of the following suggest impending eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Polyuria with a urine output above 200 mL per hour
Persistent frontal headache that does not respond to simple analgesia
Blurring of vision, scotomata or photophobia
Vomiting with severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
questions.exp: Oliguria, not polyuria, accompanies severe disease; headache, visual disturbance and epigastric pain are the classic warning symptoms. (Book p392)

questions.q: Fill up: The notes state that all women with pre-eclampsia should be ______.
opts: Observed at home without any tests
Managed on an OPD basis only
Discharged after a single blood-pressure reading
questions.exp: The notes state that all pre-eclampsia patients should be admitted. (Book p392)

questions.q: Which statement about the investigations emphasised in all pre-eclampsia patients is TRUE?
opts: Liver function tests, serum creatinine and platelet count are the three highlighted tests
Karyotyping, TORCH serology and VDRL are the three highlighted tests
Serum bile acids, indirect Coombs test and OGTT are the three highlighted tests
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, calcium and HbA1c are the three highlighted tests
questions.exp: LFT, serum creatinine and platelet count are the three investigations highlighted for every pre-eclampsia patient. (Book p392)

questions.q: Fill up: Eclampsia is called atypical when convulsions occur before ______ weeks of gestation or more than ______ after delivery.
questions.exp: Eclampsia before 20 weeks or beyond 48 hours postpartum is atypical and should prompt a search for another cause such as a cerebral lesion. (Book p392)

questions.q: Which statement about Eclampsia — Eclampsia severe PE is TRUE?
opts: Proteinuria without hypertension is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Chronic hypertension with edema only is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Severe pre-eclampsia with generalized tonic-clonic seizures is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
Any seizure in a pregnant woman with normal BP is the listed eclampsia as per the notes
questions.exp: Eclampsia is severe PE plus generalized tonic-clonic seizures. (Book p393)

questions.q: A 26-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure before the onset of labour pain. Which type of eclampsia is this, and what is its prognosis?
opts: Antepartum eclampsia, the commonest type and the worst prognosis
Intrapartum eclampsia, the commonest type and the worst prognosis
Postpartum eclampsia, which is uncommon and has the best prognosis
Atypical eclampsia, needing anticonvulsants for six months
questions.exp: Antepartum eclampsia is the most common type and has the worst prognosis; postpartum eclampsia is within 48 hours of delivery and onset beyond 48 hours is atypical. (Book p393)

questions.q: Fill up: Postpartum eclampsia occurs after delivery ______.
questions.exp: Postpartum eclampsia occurs after delivery within 48 hours. (Book p393)

questions.q: Match the atypical eclampsia with the correct detail — 1) seizure timing is atypical for eclampsia 2) antenatal seizure timing should be considered atypical eclampsia 3) is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia … A) More than 48 hours after delivery B) Before 20 weeks of pregnancy C) MRI
questions.exp: Onset beyond 48 hours postpartum is a feature of atypical eclampsia. (Book p393)

questions.q: Which statement about Atypical eclampsia — seizure before 20 is TRUE?
opts: During the second stage of labor is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
At 40 weeks only is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
Before 20 weeks of pregnancy is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
After 37 weeks is the listed atypical eclampsia as per the notes
questions.exp: A seizure before 20 weeks is an atypical-eclampsia feature. (Book p393)

questions.q: Which statement about Atypical eclampsia — MRI investigation of is TRUE?
opts: Plain abdominal X-ray is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
DIPSI is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
Kleihauer–Betke test is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
MRI is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia
questions.exp: MRI is the investigation of choice for atypical eclampsia. (Book p393)

questions.q: A 30-year-old G3P1L1 at 11 weeks gestation presents for antenatal evaluation and counselling regarding pres. According to the notes, pRES is described as edema localized to the posterior cerebral hemisphere. What is the most appropriate counselling for this patient?
opts: Advise that posterior cerebral hemisphere is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
Advise that pituitary gland is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
Advise that cerebellar vermis only is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
Advise that frontal sinus is the correct pres for this patient at this gestation
questions.exp: PRES is described as edema localized to the posterior cerebral hemisphere. (Book p393)

questions.q: Which statement about Gestational hypertension — source states that is TRUE?
opts: The source states that about 0% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 50% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 5% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
The source states that about 100% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE
questions.exp: The source states that about 50% of gestational hypertension cases evolve to PE. (Book p393)

questions.q: How should gestational hypertension with BP at least 160/110 mmHg be managed?
questions.exp: Severe-range gestational hypertension is managed like severe PE. (Book p393)

questions.q: A woman first found hypertensive after 20 weeks has no proteinuria or end-organ damage. What is the provisional diagnosis?
questions.exp: The provisional diagnosis is gestational hypertension; BP is rechecked 12 weeks after delivery. (Book p393)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: PRES causes headache, visual loss and seizures with occipital vasogenic oedema on MRI, and is managed by blood pressure control and seizure control
PRES is a haemorrhagic stroke that needs immediate neurosurgical decompression
PRES occurs only in eclampsia and is never seen in non-obstetric patients
PRES is treated with thrombolysis if the patient presents within the therapeutic window
questions.exp: PRES is vasogenic rather than haemorrhagic, is reversible with control of pressure and seizures, and also occurs with immunosuppressants and renal disease. (Book p393)

questions.q: What is the role of extravillous trophoblast in normal pregnancy?
opts: It constricts spiral arteries to reduce placental flow
It replaces spiral-artery lining and converts high-resistance vessels to low-resistance vessels
questions.exp: Extravillous trophoblast replaces spiral-artery lining, converting high-resistance arteries to low-resistance vessels. (Book p394)

questions.q: Why is spiral-artery remodeling important in normal pregnancy?
questions.exp: Trophoblastic invasion and vascular remodeling maintain uteroplacental circulation. (Book p394)

questions.q: When does the first phase of normal spiral-artery remodeling occur and what segment is replaced?
opts: At 12 weeks; the decidual segment lining
questions.exp: The first phase occurs around 12 weeks and replaces the decidual segment lining. (Book p394)

questions.q: When does the second phase of normal spiral-artery remodeling occur and what segment is replaced?
opts: At 16–20 weeks; the myometrial segment lining
questions.exp: The second phase is 16–20 weeks and replaces the myometrial segment lining. (Book p394)

questions.q: Which maternal immune cell type participates in spiral-artery remodeling?
questions.exp: Maternal NK cells play a role in vascular remodeling. (Book p394)

questions.q: What is incomplete in trophoblastic invasion in PIH according to the notes?
questions.exp: In PIH, the second phase of trophoblastic invasion is incomplete. (Book p394)

questions.q: What happens to spiral-artery resistance when trophoblastic remodeling is incomplete?
opts: It becomes unrelated to placental blood flow
questions.exp: Incomplete invasion leaves resistance high. (Book p394)

questions.q: What immediate placental consequence follows persistently high spiral-artery resistance?
opts: Reduced blood volume in the intervillous space and placental ischemia
questions.exp: High resistance lowers intervillous blood volume, producing placental ischemia. (Book p394)

questions.q: Fill up: Trophoblast normally converts spiral arteries into ______ vessels, and in pre-eclampsia this conversion fails to reach the ______ segment.
questions.exp: Failed remodelling of the myometrial segment leaves high-resistance vessels, so the placenta is under-perfused and releases anti-angiogenic factors. (Book p394)

questions.q: How does placental ischemia affect placental size in the source pathway?
opts: It has no effect on placenta
questions.exp: Placental ischemia decreases placental size and contributes to uteroplacental insufficiency. (Book p395)

questions.q: What fetal growth consequence follows uteroplacental insufficiency in PIH?
questions.exp: Reduced fetal blood supply causes IUGR. (Book p395)

questions.q: Why can oligohydramnios develop in PIH with placental insufficiency?
opts: Fetal brain sparing reduces renal blood flow, causing oliguria
Maternal insulin crosses and stops urine formation
Placental ischemia increases fetal renal blood flow
questions.exp: Brain sparing directs blood to brain and away from kidneys, causing oliguria and oligohydramnios. (Book p395)

questions.q: Which mediator is increased in PIH and is an antiangiogenic soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase?
questions.exp: sFlt-1 is increased and is a key antiangiogenic/vasoconstrictor mediator. (Book p395)

questions.q: Which pair of vasodilatory/angiogenic mediators is decreased in PIH?
questions.exp: VEGF and placental growth factor are decreased in PIH. (Book p395)

questions.q: Which eicosanoid change favors vasoconstriction in PIH?
opts: Decreased thromboxane A2 with increased prostacyclin I2
Increased thromboxane A2 with decreased prostacyclin I2
questions.exp: PIH shifts toward increased thromboxane A2 and decreased prostacyclin I2. (Book p395)

questions.q: What happens to sensitivity to angiotensin in PIH?
questions.exp: PIH features increased sensitivity to angiotensin. (Book p395)

questions.q: Match the mediator with its role in pre-eclampsia — 1) Excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 2) Placental growth factor 3) Endothelin-1 … A) Falls in pre-eclampsia and forms the denominator of the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio B) Antagonises VEGF and PlGF, producing endothelial dysfunction and proteinuria C) A powerful vasoconstrictor released from damaged endothelium
questions.exp: sFlt-1 excess neutralises VEGF and PlGF, PlGF falls and endothelin rises, producing vasoconstriction, capillary leak and proteinuria. (Book p395)

questions.q: What is the first clinical manifestation of PIH following vasoconstriction?
questions.exp: Vasoconstriction causes raised BP, the first clinical manifestation after 20 weeks. (Book p395)

questions.q: What does endothelial injury do to capillaries in PIH?
opts: Makes them impermeable to all fluid
questions.exp: Endothelial injury makes capillaries leaky. (Book p395)

questions.q: What third-space manifestations follow capillary leak in PIH?
questions.exp: Capillary leak moves fluid to the third space, causing pathological edema and ascites. (Book p395)

questions.q: What intravascular state follows capillary leak in PIH?
questions.exp: Fluid loss from vessels causes hemoconcentration. (Book p395)

questions.q: Which three elements form the Virchow-triad pathway in PIH noted in the source?
opts: Stasis, platelet activation/aggregation, and endothelial injury
questions.exp: Stasis, platelet activation/aggregation, and endothelial injury raise thrombosis risk. (Book p395)

questions.q: What major systemic result can occur from PIH-associated thrombosis?
questions.exp: Thrombosis can lead to end-organ damage and multiple-organ failure. (Book p395)

questions.q: What is described as the main factor in PIH pathophysiology?
questions.exp: The placenta is the main factor; PIH can occur even with no fetus, as in molar pregnancy. (Book p396)

questions.q: All of the following are features of severe pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Haemoconcentration with a rising platelet count
Systolic blood pressure of 160 mmHg or more on two occasions
Proteinuria of 5 g or more in 24 hours
Oliguria with a serum creatinine above 1.2 mg/dL
questions.exp: Thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration go together; a rising platelet count is not a feature of severe disease. (Book p396)

questions.q: What is the definitive treatment for PIH?
questions.exp: Delivery/termination of pregnancy is the definitive treatment. (Book p396)

questions.q: What is the first organ involved in PIH and what is its characteristic histology?
questions.exp: The maternal kidney is first involved, showing glomeruloendotheliosis. (Book p396)

questions.q: What happens to renal blood flow and GFR in PIH?
opts: Renal blood flow increases while GFR falls
questions.exp: Raised BP and renal involvement reduce renal blood flow and GFR. (Book p396)

questions.q: Which laboratory pattern follows reduced renal filtration in PIH?
opts: Raised serum urea, uric acid, and creatinine
Low creatinine with low uric acid
questions.exp: Reduced filtration raises serum urea, uric acid, and creatinine. (Book p396)

questions.q: Which process can lead from leaky cerebral capillary endothelium to eclamptic seizures?
opts: Improved autoregulation and reduced blood flow
Cerebral edema, hypoxia, and excitatory-neurotransmitter release
questions.exp: Leaky cerebral capillaries lead to edema, hypoxia, excitatory neurotransmitters, and convulsions. (Book p396)

questions.q: Loss of cerebral autoregulation in PIH produces what hemodynamic consequence?
questions.exp: Loss of autoregulation causes cerebral hyperperfusion. (Book p396)

questions.q: Why do visual disturbances occur in PIH according to the notes?
opts: Cerebral hyperperfusion affects the occipital lobe
The retina is replaced by trophoblast
Maternal insulin crosses the optic nerve
questions.exp: Cerebral hyperperfusion chiefly involving the occipital lobe explains visual disturbance. (Book p396)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about death from severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: Intracerebral haemorrhage is the commonest cause of death, which is why severe hypertension must be treated
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the commonest cause of death in eclampsia
Pulmonary embolism is the leading cause of maternal death in pre-eclampsia
Acute fatty liver is the usual terminal event, with profound hypoglycaemia
questions.exp: Cerebral haemorrhage from uncontrolled hypertension kills most women with fatal eclampsia; treating severe pressure prevents it. (Book p396)

questions.q: Which reproductive history represents first exposure to placenta and raises PIH risk?
opts: Multiparity with the same partner only
questions.exp: Primigravida is listed as first placental exposure and a PIH risk factor. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which paternal/spacing history raises PIH risk by exposing a woman to placenta for the first time again?
opts: A previous episiotomy and repair in an earlier delivery
Rh-positive status with a previously affected infant
New paternity, or a long interpregnancy interval
Breastfeeding alone, through sustained prolactin release
questions.exp: The 'first exposure to a new placenta' hypothesis explains why a new partner or a long gap between pregnancies raises risk. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which group is associated with PIH because of increased placental tissue/placentomegaly?
opts: Twin pregnancy, diabetes, or Rh-negative pregnancy
questions.exp: Twin pregnancy, diabetes, and Rh-negative pregnancy are listed with placentomegaly risk. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which condition illustrates early-onset pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks due to placental tissue?
questions.exp: Molar pregnancy is associated with early-onset PE before 20 weeks. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which autoimmune diseases are listed as PIH risk factors?
questions.exp: APLA syndrome and SLE are listed autoimmune PIH risks. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which maternal age group is listed as higher risk for PIH?
opts: Younger than 18 years or 40 years and older
questions.exp: The risk group is age <18 years or ≥40 years. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which patient characteristics are listed as PIH risk factors?
opts: Tall stature and normal calcium only
Obesity, calcium deficiency, and genetic predisposition
questions.exp: Obesity, calcium deficiency, and genetic predisposition are listed risk factors. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which previous history increases PIH risk?
opts: IVF, chronic hypertension, prior PIH, or chronic kidney disease
Only a prior uncomplicated vaginal birth
questions.exp: IVF, chronic HTN, PIH, and chronic kidney disease are listed risk factors. (Book p397)

questions.q: What is the protective factor listed for PIH in these source notes?
questions.exp: Smoking is listed as a protective factor in the source notes. (Book p397)

questions.q: All of the following are risk factors for pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Multiparity with a previous uncomplicated term delivery
First pregnancy or a new partner
Pre-existing hypertension, diabetes or renal disease
Family history of pre-eclampsia in the mother or a sister
questions.exp: Previous uncomplicated pregnancy protects against pre-eclampsia; primipaternity, a new partner, medical disease and family history all raise risk. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which measure has a proven role in PIH prevention?
questions.exp: Aspirin is included among measures with a proven preventive role. (Book p397)

questions.q: When do calcium supplements have a proven preventive role for PIH according to the notes?
opts: In every woman irrespective of calcium status
Only when calcium deficiency is present
questions.exp: Calcium supplements are useful only in calcium deficiency. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which measure is listed as having no proven role in PIH prevention?
questions.exp: Absolute bed rest has no proven preventive role. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which dietary strategy is listed as having no proven role in PIH prevention?
questions.exp: Salt restriction is in the no-proven-role column. (Book p397)

questions.q: Which patient group is specifically highlighted for low-dose aspirin prophylaxis?
opts: APLA syndrome, chronic HTN, multifetal pregnancy, kidney disease, or diabetes
Only women with normal BP and no risk factors
questions.exp: The mnemonic list includes APLA, chronic HTN, multifetal gestation, kidney disease, and diabetes. (Book p398)

questions.q: When should low-dose aspirin prophylaxis for PIH be started?
opts: At 12 weeks, not later than 16 weeks
questions.exp: Start aspirin at 12 weeks and no later than 16 weeks. (Book p398)

questions.q: When is low-dose aspirin stopped in the stated PIH-prevention protocol?
questions.exp: The low-dose aspirin course ends at 36 weeks. (Book p398)

questions.q: What aspirin dose range is listed for PIH prophylaxis?
questions.exp: The stated prophylactic dose range is 80–150 mg/day. (Book p398)

questions.q: Fill up: Low-dose aspirin prophylaxis is given as ______ mg daily, ideally started before ______ weeks of gestation.
questions.exp: Aspirin 75-150 mg at night started before 16 weeks and continued to delivery reduces pre-eclampsia in women at moderate or high risk. (Book p398)

questions.q: Which biomarker pattern is listed as a new predictor of PIH?
opts: Raised sFlt-1 and soluble endoglin with low VEGF and PlGF
Raised VEGF and PlGF with low sFlt-1
questions.exp: New predictors include ↑sFlt-1/soluble endoglin and ↓VEGF/placental growth factor. (Book p398)

questions.q: Which ratio is identified as the best biomarker predictor of PIH?
questions.exp: The sFlt-1:PlGF ratio is marked as the best predictor. (Book p398)

questions.q: Which is an outdated PIH predictor in the notes?
questions.exp: The roll-over test and angiotensin-II challenge test are labelled outdated predictors. (Book p398)

questions.q: What happens to the normal uterine-artery diastolic notch as pregnancy progresses?
opts: It disappears by 20–22 weeks as peripheral vascular resistance falls
It appears for the first time at 36 weeks
questions.exp: In normal pregnancy, falling PVR leads the diastolic notch to disappear by 20–22 weeks. (Book p398)

questions.q: Which uterine-artery Doppler finding predicts PIH?
opts: Persistent diastolic notch with increased PI or RI
Absent systolic flow with low PI
questions.exp: Persistence of the notch and increased pulsatility or resistance index predict PIH. (Book p398)

questions.q: At what gestational window is uterine-artery Doppler used to predict PIH?
questions.exp: The source lists 22–24 weeks to predict PIH. (Book p398)

questions.q: At what gestational window are uterine-artery PI and RI used to predict early-onset pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: PI and RI at 11–13 weeks are listed for early-onset PE prediction. (Book p398)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about uterine artery Doppler is TRUE?
opts: Persistent early diastolic notching with a high pulsatility index at 22-24 weeks predicts pre-eclampsia and growth restriction
A diastolic notch is normal up to 34 weeks and carries no predictive value
Uterine artery Doppler is a diagnostic test that confirms the presence of pre-eclampsia
A low-resistance waveform with absent notching after 24 weeks indicates placental insufficiency
questions.exp: Abnormal uterine artery waveform at the anomaly scan is a predictor rather than a diagnosis, and normal pregnancy loses the notch after 24 weeks. (Book p398)

questions.q: What is the initial disposition stated for all PIH cases in the management page?
opts: Manage all on OPD without tests
Deliver all cases immediately before assessment
questions.exp: The p399 management page begins with admission of all PIH cases. (Book p399)

questions.q: Which test set is used to help rule out HELLP syndrome in PIH?
opts: Liver enzymes, creatinine, platelets, LDH and a blood film for schistocytes
Thyroid function, a glucose tolerance test and an indirect Coombs test
A urine pregnancy test and nothing else beyond the blood pressure
Fetal karyotyping and a TORCH screen on maternal blood
questions.exp: Ruling out HELLP needs haemolysis (LDH, film), liver involvement and a platelet count, with renal function included. (Book p399)

questions.q: A PIH patient with BP above 160/110 or end-organ damage should be classified and managed as:
questions.exp: BP >160/110 or end-organ damage indicates severe PE, which remains admitted. (Book p399)

questions.q: A PIH patient without severe BP or end-organ damage is managed as:
opts: Mild pre-eclampsia on an OPD basis
questions.exp: Without severe findings, the source indicates mild PE and OPD management. (Book p399)

questions.q: At what gestation is delivery planned for mild pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: The timing table lists 37 weeks for mild PE. (Book p399)

questions.q: At what gestation is delivery planned for severe pre-eclampsia when no immediate indication is present?
questions.exp: The timing table lists 34 weeks for severe PE. (Book p399)

questions.q: Which group requires immediate termination irrespective of gestational age in the p399 table?
opts: Diet-controlled gestational diabetes at any gestation
Eclampsia, impending eclampsia, HELLP, fetal distress or abruption
Mild pre-eclampsia alone presenting before 28 weeks
Chronic hypertension alone presenting before 20 weeks
questions.exp: In the p399 table, immediate termination irrespective of gestational age is required for eclampsia, impending eclampsia, HELLP, fetal distress or abruption. (Book p399)

questions.q: When is delivery planned for chronic hypertension without superimposed pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: The table gives 37–38 weeks for chronic hypertension. (Book p399)

questions.q: When is delivery planned for chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: The timing table lists 37 weeks for chronic hypertension with superimposed PE. (Book p399)

questions.q: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia has a blood pressure of 170/115 mmHg, 3+ proteinuria, persistent headache, platelets of 110,000 and a normal CTG. Magnesium sulfate has been started. What is the plan?
opts: Control the blood pressure, give antenatal corticosteroids, and deliver once she is stabilised
Expectant management until 37 weeks whatever the severity of the disease
Immediate caesarean section before steroids or blood pressure control
Discharge her on oral nifedipine and review her as an outpatient in one week
questions.exp: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks means stabilise, give steroids, then deliver rather than either emergency intervention or prolonged expectancy. (Book p399)

questions.q: How often is daily fetal movement count done in mild and severe pre-eclampsia?
opts: Weekly in mild and never in severe
questions.exp: The table lists daily fetal movement counting for both mild and severe PE. (Book p400)

questions.q: How does NST frequency differ between mild and severe pre-eclampsia?
opts: Weekly in mild and alternate days in severe
Daily in mild and monthly in severe
Never in mild and weekly in severe
The same once-monthly schedule in both
questions.exp: NST is weekly in mild PE and alternate-day in severe PE. (Book p400)

questions.q: How does biophysical-score frequency differ between mild and severe pre-eclampsia?
opts: Weekly in mild and alternate days in severe
Daily in mild and monthly in severe
No BPS is needed in severe PE
questions.exp: BPS is weekly in mild PE and alternate-day in severe PE. (Book p400)

questions.q: How often is ultrasound for fetal growth done in mild versus severe pre-eclampsia?
opts: Only once at 20 weeks in both
Every 3 weeks in mild and every 2 weeks in severe
Every week in mild and every month in severe
questions.exp: Growth scan frequency is every 3 weeks in mild and every 2 weeks in severe PE. (Book p400)

questions.q: What umbilical-artery S/D ratio is a PIH/uteroplacental-insufficiency finding linked to delivery at 37 weeks?
questions.exp: An umbilical-artery S/D ratio ≥3 is linked to 37-week delivery in the source table. (Book p400)

questions.q: What is the listed delivery timing for absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery?
questions.exp: Absent end-diastolic flow is linked to delivery at 33–34 weeks. (Book p400)

questions.q: What is the listed delivery timing for reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery?
questions.exp: Reversed end-diastolic flow is linked to delivery at 31–32 weeks. (Book p400)

questions.q: Fill up: In fetal growth restriction, umbilical artery Doppler is the surveillance test of choice, while Doppler of the ______ detects the brain-sparing response.
questions.exp: Umbilical artery Doppler guides timing in growth restriction, and a reduced middle cerebral artery pulsatility index shows redistribution to the brain. (Book p400)

questions.q: Where is mild pre-eclampsia without severe features managed in the notes?
questions.exp: Mild PE without severe features is managed on an OPD basis. (Book p400)

questions.q: From what gestation does fetal monitoring begin in the mild-PE OPD approach?
questions.exp: The OPD approach starts fetal monitoring at 32 weeks. (Book p400)

questions.q: What counseling is specifically included for mild pre-eclampsia?
opts: Education on signs and symptoms of impending eclampsia
questions.exp: Patients are educated about impending-eclampsia signs and symptoms. (Book p400)

questions.q: What BP level is an ACOG indication for IV antihypertensives in mild/severe PE?
opts: At least 140/90 mmHg in all women
questions.exp: The source notes IV antihypertensives for BP ≥160/110 mmHg per ACOG. (Book p400)

questions.q: Which therapies have no role in mild pre-eclampsia management according to the notes?
opts: Aspirin, bed rest, salt reduction, and magnesium sulfate
questions.exp: The source lists no role for aspirin, bed rest, salt restriction, and MgSO4 in mild PE. (Book p400)

questions.q: Where is severe pre-eclampsia treated?
opts: No care is required until 39 weeks
questions.exp: Severe pre-eclampsia is treated as an inpatient. (Book p401)

questions.q: Why is magnesium sulfate used in severe pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: MgSO4 is used to prevent seizures. (Book p401)

questions.q: Why are antihypertensives used in severe pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: Antihypertensives are used to prevent intracranial hemorrhage. (Book p401)

questions.q: In severe PE without emergency conditions and at less than 34 weeks, what is the corticosteroid plan?
opts: Give aspirin alone and discharge her for outpatient review
Complete the corticosteroid course while continuing the pregnancy to 34 weeks with monitoring
Deliver the baby before the first dose of corticosteroid is given
Withhold corticosteroids, since they worsen the maternal blood pressure
questions.exp: Without an emergency indication, severe pre-eclampsia before 34 weeks is managed expectantly with a completed course of steroids and close monitoring. (Book p401)

questions.q: Which condition is an emergency indication for delivery after the first corticosteroid dose?
questions.exp: HELLP syndrome is listed among emergencies warranting delivery after the first steroid dose. (Book p401)

questions.sec: Mild PE management vs severe PE management
questions.q: Match the presentation with its management — 1) Mild pre-eclampsia at term 2) Severe pre-eclampsia before 34 weeks 3) Severe pre-eclampsia after 34 weeks … A) Delivery after stabilisation, usually within 24-48 hours B) Expectant management with steroids and magnesium in a tertiary centre C) Induction of labour and delivery, since the baby is already mature
questions.exp: Mild disease at term is delivered; severe disease before 34 weeks may be deferred only with intensive monitoring at a tertiary centre. (Book p401)

questions.q: What is the most common complication of severe pre-eclampsia listed on the management page?
questions.exp: Abruptio placentae is marked as the most common complication. (Book p401)

questions.q: What is the preferred mode of delivery in mild or severe pre-eclampsia when there is no obstetric indication for cesarean?
questions.exp: Vaginal delivery is preferred; cesarean is only for an obstetric indication. (Book p401)

questions.q: Which anesthetic technique is preferred for delivery in pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: The notes prefer neuraxial anesthesia, particularly epidural. (Book p401)

questions.q: What is the first supportive step for a woman actively convulsing from eclampsia?
opts: Raise bed rails and manage the airway
questions.exp: The algorithm begins with safety measures, raised bed rails, and airway management. (Book p401)

questions.q: After airway/safety measures, what two treatment pillars are used for eclampsia?
opts: Insulin to control blood sugar and anti-D prophylaxis
Low-dose aspirin for prevention and strict bed rest
Cervical cerclage and vaginal progesterone support
Magnesium sulfate for seizures and antihypertensives for BP
questions.exp: After airway and safety measures, eclampsia is treated with two pillars: magnesium sulfate for seizures and antihypertensives for blood pressure. (Book p401)

questions.q: What is the definitive management of eclampsia after stabilization?
opts: Observe until 40 weeks in all cases
questions.exp: After stabilization, eclampsia requires termination/delivery irrespective of gestation. (Book p401)

questions.sec: Severe PE & eclampsia: magnesium sulfate regimen
questions.q: Fill up: In the Pritchard regimen the loading dose is ______ g of magnesium sulfate intravenously plus ______ g intramuscularly.
questions.exp: Pritchard loading is 4 g intravenously and 10 g intramuscularly (5 g into each buttock), followed by 5 g intramuscularly four-hourly. (Book p401)
